title: Crowns, bridges, implants and dentures: comparing dental options
intro: A damaged or missing tooth does not have one automatic solution. A crown can protect a remaining tooth, while a bridge, an implant-supported restoration or a removable denture may replace missing teeth. The best choice depends on the health of the mouth, chewing, appearance, ability to clean, treatment burden and cost. Ask for a plan that explains the alternatives before an irreversible step.

sections.heading: Start with the tooth and the whole mouth
paragraphs: The dentist examines remaining tooth structure, roots, gums, bite and the space to be restored, using imaging when needed. Decay or gum disease may need treatment first. If a natural tooth can reasonably be retained, compare a filling, partial covering or crown with extraction and replacement. A crown covers a prepared tooth; it is not an artificial root. Preparation removes tooth tissue and may lead to sensitivity or sometimes later root-canal treatment. Ask what can be preserved and what would happen without immediate replacement. In selected gaps with little effect on function or appearance, monitoring without a replacement can be reasonable.

sections.heading: A bridge uses support beside the gap
paragraphs: A conventional bridge attaches an artificial tooth to crowns on supporting teeth. It can restore a gap without implant surgery, but usually requires reshaping the neighbouring teeth and depends on their condition. A resin-bonded bridge uses an adhesive wing and often requires much less tooth preparation; it can become unstuck and is not suitable for every bite or space. Ask why the proposed design fits your mouth and how to clean beneath it. Decay, gum problems or damage to a supporting tooth can affect the whole bridge. Fixed does not mean maintenance-free or guaranteed for life.

sections.heading: An implant supports a tooth replacement
paragraphs: An implant is placed surgically in the jawbone and can support a crown, bridge or some dentures. It avoids using adjacent teeth as supports, but needs suitable bone, oral health and a plan for healing. Bone grafting may add procedures and time when bone is insufficient. Smoking, gum disease, some medical conditions and medicines can affect suitability and risk; tell the team your full history. Possible problems include infection, failure to bond with bone and injury to nearby structures, including nerves in some sites. The visible tooth and the implant are separate components, each of which may need maintenance or replacement.

sections.heading: Removable dentures can replace several or all teeth
paragraphs: A partial denture replaces some missing teeth; a complete denture replaces the teeth in an upper or lower jaw. Some dentures gain extra stability from implants, but this still may be a removable design. Eating and speaking can take practice, and sore areas need adjustment rather than being tolerated indefinitely. An immediate denture fitted after extraction may need changes as the mouth heals. Remove and clean it as instructed and normally leave it out overnight unless the dentist advises otherwise. Clean the gums and remaining teeth as well. Do not reshape a denture yourself or glue broken parts with household glue.

sections.heading: Compare the full course, including future care
paragraphs: Request a written estimate covering assessment, temporary teeth, surgery if relevant, the final restoration, follow-up and likely maintenance. Coverage and charges vary by country and service. Ask about appointments, healing time, materials, appearance, repair options and who will provide care if treatment is elsewhere. No option lasts forever, and an implant is not exempt from gum inflammation or bone loss. Learn daily cleaning around crowns, under bridges and around implants, plus denture-specific cleaning and storage. Arrange dental review for pain, looseness, bleeding or a changing bite. A second opinion can help when options are complex or substantial healthy tooth tissue would be removed.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: protecting neighbouring teeth
examples.text: Sara has a missing front tooth and healthy teeth beside the gap. She asks why a conventional bridge was proposed and whether a resin-bonded bridge, implant or removable option would suit her. The dentist compares the bite, preparation, treatment time and cost instead of assuming one design is best for everyone.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: planning beyond the fitting day
examples.text: A man considering an implant asks whether the quoted price includes the crown, possible grafting and future checks. He also learns how to clean it and who would repair a loose component. This helps him compare a complete treatment plan with alternatives rather than only the advertised implant price.

questions: Can my natural tooth be retained, and what tissue would each option remove?
How do the alternatives compare for surgery, cleaning, time and repair?
What does the written price include, and who handles future problems?
